definition: The program whose whole job is listening to your keyboard in a terminal. It reads each line, decides what you meant, and runs it — a translator between you and your computer, not magic.
The window where you type commands. Once a physical device, now an app that pretends to be one — the shell lives inside it.
The physical global network — undersea cables, routers, data centres — that carries data between computers. The road. The web is just one vehicle that uses it.
Short for World Wide Web — the system of hyperlinked pages, URLs, and HTTP that runs on top of the internet. Invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, given away for free.
A small chunk of data — a few hundred to about 1,500 bytes — sent independently with an address header and reassembled on arrival. Nothing on the internet travels as one piece.
A unique number identifying a device on the network, like a house address for packets. Your public IP changes; private IPs live inside your home network.
The original addressing system — four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots. About 4.3 billion addresses; the pool ran dry in 2011.
The modern addressing system — long hexadecimal addresses with room for so many devices that every grain of sand on Earth could have one.
The protocol that guarantees delivery: confirms the connection, acknowledges every packet, re-sends lost ones, and reorders arrivals. IP's responsible older sibling.
A fast protocol that makes zero promises — no handshake, no re-sending. Used where speed beats perfection: video calls, games, live streams.
The device that directs packets between networks — the traffic cop of the internet. In your home, it also translates public and private IP addresses (NAT).
Network Address Translation — the trick that lets one public IP address serve every device on your home network by translating between outside and inside addresses.
The 1969 US defense research network built to survive a nuclear attack — the internet's ancestor, and the reason the internet has no centre.
Whatever initiates a request. A browser, an app, curl, a Python script — even another server. Not a type of machine; a role in the conversation.
Whatever listens for requests and answers them. Not a special machine — any computer told to sit and wait. Your laptop becomes one when you run a dev server.
The web's fundamental relationship: one side always asks (client), one side always answers (server). Asymmetric by design — the server never initiates.
The client's half of the conversation: 'may I have this thing?' A message asking a server for data or an action.
The server's half of the conversation: the answer to a request — the data asked for, or an explanation of why it couldn't be done.
'This computer, right here.' A loopback address where client and server are the same machine — the whole market stall happening inside your laptop during development.
A network model with no fixed server — every machine is both client and server, talking directly. BitTorrent and blockchain work this way. The web does not.
A client that does almost no work itself — it just displays what the server sends. The early web's browser: fully-rendered HTML arrives, the browser shows it.
A client that does the heavy lifting itself — the server sends data, the client assembles the interface. Modern SPAs like Gmail and Twitter.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — the text-based rules for how clients and servers speak: a method, a path, headers, sometimes a body. Not a program you install; a language you agree to speak.
HTTP wrapped in TLS encryption — same messages, same format, unreadable to anyone listening in the middle. The S stands for Secure; the padlock is its promise.
The verb that opens every HTTP request — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE — declaring what kind of action you want before the server reads anything else.
The three-digit number every HTTP response starts with — 200, 404, 500 — summarising how the request went. Programs read the number; the words after it are just for humans.
A key: value line carrying context about an HTTP message — who's asking, what format they accept, how long to cache, which site they mean. Metadata, not payload.
The payload of an HTTP message — the HTML, JSON, or bytes actually being transferred. Optional in requests, almost always present in responses.
Uniform Resource Locator — the address of a resource on the web. What you type into the address bar; what the path in a request names.
Transport Layer Security — the encryption protocol under HTTPS. Fixed SSL's flaws in 1999 and has been the real protocol ever since, even though everyone still says SSL.
Secure Sockets Layer — Netscape's 1990s encryption protocol, retired for its vulnerabilities. The name outlived the technology: say TLS if you want to be precise.
A server's digital ID card, checked by your browser during the TLS handshake — proof that this server is really the domain it claims, not an impersonator.
The convention mapping numbers to characters — which byte means which letter. Every text file has one, declared or not; get it wrong and the bytes misread as garbage.
The web's universal character encoding — variable-length, covering every human language plus emoji. Plain English costs one byte per letter; everything else costs more.
The declared character encoding of a document — the charset=utf-8 half of a Content-Type header. One small string deciding whether a page reads beautifully or renders as mojibake.
Garbage text produced by reading bytes with the wrong encoding — Ã© instead of é. From the Japanese 文字化け, 'character transformation.' Not corruption; just the wrong key.

The four-step rhythm of every conversation on the web: the client asks, the server processes, the server answers, the client receives. Repeat it a few billion times a second and you have the internet.

Domain Name System — the internet's phone book. It translates human-friendly domain names into the IP addresses machines actually use, with caches at every level so repeat lookups cost almost nothing.
The three-message ritual — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — that opens a TCP connection before any data flows. Every handshake costs a round trip.
Another name for the TCP handshake: three messages, one agreement to talk, paid for in a single round trip.
The negotiation that runs after TCP connects, in which the server proves its identity with a certificate and both sides agree on encryption keys. HTTPS pays for it on every new connection.
The delay before data arrives, usually measured as the round-trip time between client and server. Distance, handshakes and slow processing all add to it.
One full journey: a message out to the server and a reply back. Handshakes are priced in round trips, and physical distance multiplies their cost.

A stored copy kept close by, so a request can be answered without repeating the full journey. Browsers, operating systems, routers, DNS servers, CDNs and backends all keep caches. The fastest request is the one never made.

Time To First Byte — the moment the server's first byte of response arrives, marking the boundary between the connection phase and the server's thinking phase. High TTFB means the backend is the problem.
